# Where the Last Two Lectures Ran Out

Two architectures, two different ways of failing to see time.

---

## Two Architectures That Cannot See Time

Lecture 7 gave you a feedforward network. It treats each row independently — everything it knows about *when* something happened, you encoded by hand as a lag column. Shuffle the features and the model is unchanged.

Lecture 8 gave you a 1D CNN, which does see local shape. But its **receptive field** is fixed by architecture: stacked width-5 and width-3 filters reach about seven weeks back, and no reasonable stack of small filters reaches an annual lag. Worse, pooling deliberately discarded *where* in the window each pattern occurred — and we measured that costing about 500 RMSE.

::: {.keybox}
Both architectures share one assumption: the input is a **fixed-size block** to be processed all at once. Neither has any notion of reading a sequence *in order* and carrying something forward.
:::

That is the gap today closes.

---

## The Recurrent Idea: Carry State Forward

A recurrent network reads the sequence one step at a time and maintains a **hidden state** $\mathbf{h}_t$ — a running summary of everything seen so far.

At each step it does two things: update the summary using the new input *and* the previous summary, then optionally emit an output. The same weights are used at every step, which is weight sharing again — along time rather than along space.

**The consequence worth sitting with.** There is no fixed window. In principle $\mathbf{h}_t$ encodes the entire history $x_1, \ldots, x_t$, so the architecture imposes no limit on how far back the model can look.

**In principle.** Most of this lecture is about the gap between that promise and what a recurrent network actually delivers — and about the architecture built to close it.

# The Vanilla RNN

One equation, applied over and over — and the reason that is both the whole idea and the whole problem.

---

## Vanilla RNN: One Equation, Repeated

::: {.definitionbox}
::: {.definitionbox-title}
The recurrence
:::
$$\mathbf{h}_t = \tanh\!\left(\mathbf{W}_h \mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{W}_x \mathbf{x}_t + \mathbf{b}\right),
\qquad \hat{y}_t = \mathbf{W}_y \mathbf{h}_t + \mathbf{b}_y$$
:::

![](../Figures/Lecture09_Part1/unrolled_rnn.svg){fig-align="center" height="230px"}

In words: the new summary is a squashed mix of the old summary and the new week. Shared weights mean a 26-week window costs no more parameters than a 5-week one — about **4,500** here, against 22,657 for Lecture 7's network.

---

## Training It: Backpropagation Through Time

Training an RNN is ordinary backpropagation applied to an unusual graph. **Unroll** the recurrence across the window and it becomes a 26-layer feedforward network — one layer per time step — in which every layer shares the same weights.

Gradients then flow backward from the loss at step $T$ all the way to step 1. Because $\mathbf{W}_h$ appears at every step, its gradient is a *sum* of contributions from all 26 positions.

::: {.warningbox}
**This is where it breaks.** Propagating a gradient back through $k$ steps multiplies by roughly $\mathbf{W}_h$ $k$ times. If the relevant factor is below 1, the gradient shrinks *exponentially*; above 1, it can explode. Either way, long-range signal does not survive the trip.
:::

Exploding gradients have an easy fix — `clip_grad_norm_` caps the size of the update, and we use it. Vanishing gradients do not, which is what the next section is for.

---

## Why a Vanilla RNN Forgets

Suppose each backward step multiplies the gradient by $0.7$ — an unremarkable value for a $\tanh$ network — and compare our own trained RNN, measured [@Bengio1994]:

![](../Figures/Lecture09_Part1/gradient_decay.svg){fig-align="center" height="330px"}

**The same factor every step is a straight line on a log scale.** Ours keeps about $0.79$ a step: **0.4%** of the gradient reaches 26 weeks back, **0.001%** the same week last year. **Bengio and colleagues** proved this is inherent to the architecture.

# LSTM: Long Short-Term Memory

Add a memory that information passes through rather than being recomputed at every step.

---

## LSTM: A Cell State and Three Gates

An LSTM carries **two** things forward: a **cell state** $\mathbf{c}_t$, which is the long-term memory, and a **hidden state** $\mathbf{h}_t$, which is what the rest of the network sees. Three gates control the traffic between them [@Hochreiter1997; @Gers2000].

| | |
|---|---|
| **Forget gate** | $\mathbf{f}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_f[\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_f)$ — what fraction of the old memory to keep |
| **Input gate** | $\mathbf{i}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_i[\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_i)$ — how much of the new candidate to write |
| **Output gate** | $\mathbf{o}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_o[\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_o)$ — how much of memory to expose |

The memory update itself is the line that matters:

$$\mathbf{c}_t = \mathbf{f}_t \odot \mathbf{c}_{t-1} \;+\; \mathbf{i}_t \odot \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_t,
\qquad \mathbf{h}_t = \mathbf{o}_t \odot \tanh(\mathbf{c}_t)$$

Each gate is a sigmoid, so it outputs between 0 and 1 — a soft switch the network learns.

---

## What the Gates Are Doing, in Plain Terms

The equations are compact but the behavior is intuitive. Take a store forecasting demand week by week.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Forget** | "The promotion that ran three months ago no longer explains anything — drop it." The gate closes toward 0 and that part of memory decays away. |
| **Input** | "This week is Thanksgiving and the spike is enormous — record it." The gate opens toward 1 and the event is written into the cell. |
| **Output** | "I am holding a memory of last December, but this week is April — do not act on it yet." Information stays in $\mathbf{c}_t$ without contaminating the current prediction. |

**The output gate is the one people skip, and it is the subtle one.** It separates *what the model remembers* from *what the model uses right now*. A vanilla RNN cannot make that distinction — its single hidden state has to serve both jobs at once, so anything it stores is immediately in play.

---

## Why the Cell State Fixes the Gradient

Follow a gradient backward through $\mathbf{c}_t = \mathbf{f}_t \odot \mathbf{c}_{t-1} + \mathbf{i}_t \odot \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_t$. Repeated multiplication shrinks; repeated addition does not.

![](../Figures/Lecture09_Part1/cell_lanes.svg){fig-align="center" height="250px"}

::: {.keybox}
**You have seen this fix before:** Lecture 8's skip connection, $\mathbf{y} = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}) + \mathbf{x}$. The 1997 LSTM had no forget gate, so its cell path *was* that identity, eighteen years before ResNet; the forget gate (2000) made it learnable.
:::

[On our panel the median forget gate is 0.52, so 7% survives four weeks. Check 2 says why.]{.neutral .smaller}

# In PyTorch, and Does It Work

Four lines of model code, and an honest measurement against everything else this course has fitted.

---

## LSTM for Forecasting in PyTorch

::: {.examplebox}
::: {.examplebox-title}
Window in, one forecast out
:::
```python
class LSTMForecaster(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_features, hidden=64, layers=1):
        super().__init__()
        self.lstm = nn.LSTM(n_features, hidden, num_layers=layers,
                            batch_first=True)
        self.fc = nn.Linear(hidden, 1)

    def forward(self, x):        # x: (batch, seq_len, n_features)
        out, (h, c) = self.lstm(x)
        return self.fc(out[:, -1, :]).squeeze(-1)
```
:::

`batch_first=True` gives shape `(batch, seq_len, features)` — the *opposite* of `Conv1d`. `out[:, -1, :]` is the state after the last step. Lecture 7's rules still hold, plus `clip_grad_norm_(..., 1.0)`.

---

## Does It Work? The Scoreboard So Far

Same weekly panel, same 26-week windows, same test block as Homework 4.

| Model | Test RMSE | Parameters |
|---|---:|---:|
| LASSO, 46 engineered features | **744** | 46 |
| XGBoost, 46 engineered features | 781 | — |
| **Vanilla RNN**, 4 raw channels | **842** | 4,545 |
| Random forest | 899 | — |
| **LSTM**, 4 raw channels | 987 | 17,985 |
| 1D CNN, best variant | 1,032 | 8,161 |
| Seasonal naive | 2,152 | 0 |

[**Recurrence beats convolution decisively**]{.key-result} — and it did so on *four raw channels* with no lag engineering at all, against 46 hand-built features for LASSO. That is the case for reading a sequence in order, in one line.

**And the LSTM lost to the vanilla RNN** — at a fixed 30-epoch budget. That is not a typo, and the next three slides are about what it does and does not mean.

---

## Why the Gated Model Lost at 30 Epochs

The result holds at all three window lengths. That rules out a fluke of one *window* — though all three rows share one panel and one split, so it is one finding measured three ways, not three independent tests:

| Window | Vanilla RNN | LSTM | |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| 13 weeks | **878** | 990 | RNN wins |
| 26 weeks | **842** | 987 | RNN wins |
| 52 weeks | **805** | 998 | RNN wins |

**An LSTM solves a problem this data does not have.** Gating preserves information across *long* dependency chains, and weekly demand is dominated by the recent past.

The gates are not free: **17,985 parameters against 4,545**. But before concluding that they bought nothing, a table like this one owes two checks — **was the comparison fair**, and **what in the data explains it**. The next two slides run both.

::: {.warningbox}
A margin measured at one training budget is a claim about that budget. We chose 30 epochs because it is the default, not because it was shown to be enough for both models.
:::

---

## Check 1: Was It a Fair Fight?

Bigger models converge slower, and the LSTM has 4× the parameters. Vary the **budget**:

![](../Figures/Lecture09_Part1/budget_curve.svg){fig-align="center" height="330px"}

::: {.keybox}
At 30 epochs the RNN wins by a wide margin. By 100 the two **tie**, and the LSTM is still improving: we ran out of patience, not the model. The RNN's real edge is speed — **three times faster on a quarter of the parameters** — not a verdict on gating.
:::

---

## Check 2: What in the Data Explains It

Gating pays when a value must survive many steps that would otherwise overwrite it. Three measurements say this panel has no such structure.

**1. Most variance is not sequential.** **91%** of the variation in weekly units is *between* series — which store, which category — and 9% is within a series over time. The main task is reading the level, and the last few weeks give you that.

**2. The series are smooth.** Within-series autocorrelation is **0.83** at lag 1 and still **0.43** at lag 52. That is why long memory is unnecessary rather than why it is needed: the recent past is a *sufficient statistic* for the distant past. Nothing must be carried across a gap, because the gap was filled in continuously.

**3. Nothing in the inputs arrives early.** `snap_days` correlates +0.14 with units in the same week; its −0.13 and +0.12 two and four weeks ahead only echo that through the monthly SNAP calendar. `event_days` is flat everywhere. No *announcement* structure — and that is precisely what a forget gate is for.

::: {.keybox}
Ask these three of your own series before reaching for a gated model: how much of my variance is cross-sectional? Is my series smooth enough that recent values already summarize old ones? Does anything in my inputs **lead** the target?
:::

# Key Takeaways

What recurrence buys, what it costs, and what is still missing.

---

## RNN and LSTM in Context

| Architecture | Sees order? | Effective memory | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| FFN on lags | no | whatever you engineered | cheap |
| 1D CNN | local only | receptive field ($\sim$7 steps) | cheap |
| Vanilla RNN | yes | $\sim$10–30 steps in practice | cheap |
| LSTM | yes | hundreds of steps | 4$\times$ an RNN |

An LSTM holds roughly **four times** the parameters of a vanilla RNN at the same hidden size — each of the three gates plus the candidate needs its own weight matrix. That is the price of the memory, and on a short window you pay it for nothing.

**What is still missing.** An LSTM reads strictly left to right, one step at a time, so it cannot be parallelized across the sequence, and everything it knows about step 3 must survive being squeezed through every state between 3 and $T$. Part 2 removes both constraints.

---

## Lecture 9 Part 1: Key Takeaways

::: {.keybox}
1. A **recurrent network** reads a sequence in order and carries a hidden state. Weights are shared across time, so window length costs no parameters.

2. Training is **backpropagation through time**: unroll the recurrence and it is a deep network whose layers share weights. Repeated multiplication shrinks the gradient exponentially — at 52 steps, around $10^{-8}$.

3. An **LSTM** adds a cell state updated **additively**. Addition preserves gradients where multiplication destroys them — the ResNet fix, eighteen years earlier.

4. Three gates: **forget** what is stale, **input** what is new, **output** what is relevant now.

5. On our panel both recurrent models **beat every CNN variant** on four raw channels — and both still lose to a 46-coefficient LASSO.

6. The **LSTM lost to the vanilla RNN at a 30-epoch budget**, at all three window lengths — but the two **tie** once both are trained to convergence, and 91% of this panel's variance is cross-sectional anyway. Gating solves long-range forgetting; this data does not suffer from it. **Fit the architecture to the problem — and check that a margin survives the budget you measured it at.**
:::
